_about: Every visitor-facing string of the Readiness Check. Templates use {name} placeholders filled by src/lib/lab/readiness.ts and the page. British English, no dashes, no score language, and no source words: a source's own words reach the page only in a review build opened with ?review=1 (src/lib/site/review.ts). Keys the server alone renders (question, lede, description, minutes, noscript, elements, next and method) are not sent to the island. statusPhrase, kindLabel and targetsNote are also read by the guide pages, through src/lib/site/prepare-hub.ts.

copy.method1: The Readiness Check draws on the EU coordinated implementation roadmap of the NIS Cooperation Group and its FAQ, the UK NCSC's migration timelines and its Next steps white paper, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security's roadmap ITSM.40.001, ANSSI's FAQ on post-quantum cryptography, the CISA, NSA and NIST quantum-readiness factsheet, and the Dutch PQC Migration Handbook by AIVD, CWI and TNO. Each question is one action a guide asks for, in the Atlas's words, with a link to the guide. {checked}
copy.checkedOn: The source's words behind each question were read and checked on {date}.
copy.checkedBetween: The source's words behind each question were read and checked between {first} and {last}.
copy.checkedNone: Each question rests on the source's own words.
copy.method2: Every date is a target. The EU roadmap is a recommendation, the NCSC, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and the other issuers publish guidance, and ANSSI says its recommendations carry no regulatory obligation today outside the areas French rules already cover. A question shows another guide's target date only where that date names the same step, completing the migration for one.
copy.method3: The guides write for different readers. The EU roadmap addresses Member States and their national roadmaps; its FAQ says entities in scope of NIS2, public administrations and critical infrastructure providers among them, should at a minimum take four of the First Steps (an inventory of cryptographic assets, dependency maps, involving the supply chain and a quantum risk analysis), and encourages every organisation to. The Canadian roadmap is written for federal departments and their non-classified systems, and the NCSC timelines mainly for large organisations, critical national infrastructure and bespoke IT. Where a question turns a national or sectoral step into an organisational one, its More says so.
copy.method4: There is no score, percentage or overall reading. The assessment sorts your own answers group by group and counts them only inside a group. The guides do not weigh their actions against each other, and a total would add a judgement none of them makes.
copy.method5: Take these first lists up to three steps you marked in progress or not started, by the earliest target date your chosen guides set for each, then those with no target date. It orders by date alone and weighs nothing else.
copy.method6: The order of the groups is not a sequence. The EU roadmap says its prepare, plan and act steps are not consecutive phases, and its FAQ says the Next Steps need not wait for the First Steps, nor planning for a complete inventory. The Canadian roadmap expects its phases to overlap, and the Dutch Handbook advises against waiting for one step to finish before starting the next. The CEPS Task Force report on the EU transition makes the same case, recommending modular packages that can start independently instead of a rigid sequence (Pupillo et al., 2025).
